speaker: J. Kenji López-Alt
title: S1E3 Celebrity Chef J. Kenji López-Alt
question: In meat preparation, what actually happens to different marinade ingredients when you marinate a thick cut of meat overnight?
guest: Marinades penetrate extremely slowly. If you take a chicken breast and you marinate it, things like salt, some simple sugars, and MSG—very small molecules—will work their way into the meat relatively fast over the course of a few hours. But big organic compounds, like the things that give you what I would think of as the harmonies of flavor, like the aroma—aromatic compounds from herbs, garlic, things like that—those are really big molecules that don't penetrate very quickly at all. So even over the course of a day, it'll penetrate a millimeter or two into the meat. If you take a chicken breast and marinate it with 40 cloves of garlic in a soy sauce solution, the salt and MSG from the soy sauce will get into the middle of the chicken relatively fast, but the garlic will only make it onto the outer layer. So if you take that chicken and carefully shave off the outer layer and cook it, you won't really even taste the garlic at all.

points.core: Small molecules like salt diffuse into meat centers within a few hours.
points.note: Accept: salt, simple sugars, or MSG penetrating deeply into meat over several hours due to small molecular size. Do not credit: claiming all marinade flavors penetrate equally.

points.core: Large aromatic organic compounds penetrate only one to two millimeters overnight.
points.note: Accept: garlic, herbs, spices, or large aromatic molecules staying within roughly 1–2 mm or a thin outer surface layer even after a full day. Do not credit: vague 'marinades stay on the outside' without contrasting large aromatics against small molecules.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Most of a marinade stays at the surface; even overnight, only a few ingredients get meaningfully inside a thick cut.

Salt is the main exception. Its small ions diffuse steadily inward, reaching perhaps a centimetre or more overnight, where they dissolve some muscle proteins and help the meat hold moisture and taste seasoned throughout. Soy sauce, fish sauce and other salty liquids work largely for this reason. Sugar and small acid molecules also move in, but more slowly and only a few millimetres.

Acids (vinegar, citrus, wine, yogurt) denature surface proteins. Brief exposure can tenderise slightly, but overnight a strong acid tends to make the outer layer mushy or chalky while the interior is unchanged. Enzymes from pineapple, papaya, kiwi or ginger are large molecules that act similarly at the surface, turning it pasty if left too long.

Oil doesn't penetrate at all, since meat is roughly 75% water; it mainly carries fat-soluble flavours and helps browning. Most aroma compounds from garlic, herbs and spices are too large to travel far, so they flavour only the outer few millimetres.

In practice, a marinade is a surface treatment plus a brine.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
When a thick cut of meat marinates overnight, almost everything except salt remains near the surface. Salt dissolves into tiny sodium and chloride ions that diffuse deep into the water-rich muscle tissue, loosening myosin proteins so the meat retains far more moisture when cooked. By contrast, flavor compounds from garlic, herbs, spices, and oils are large or fat-soluble molecules that cannot navigate tightly packed, watery muscle fibers; even overnight, they penetrate only one to three millimeters, seasoning the outer crust rather than the center. Sugars are likewise too large to travel inward, staying on the exterior where they later enhance browning and caramelization.

Acids and enzymes also act near the surface. Strong acids in vinegar, citrus, or wine penetrate just a few millimeters and denature proteins; overnight, those proteins coagulate tightly and squeeze out water, turning the exterior chalky or mushy, whereas dairy’s gentler lactic acid tenderizes more gradually. Meanwhile, protease enzymes from ingredients like pineapple, papaya, or ginger break down surface muscle fibers into a pasty layer without ever reaching the core.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Even overnight, most of a marinade never gets far past the surface of a thick cut. Meat is about 75% water and its muscle fibers are tightly packed, so ingredients move in mainly by slow diffusion, typically only a few millimeters in a day.

Salt is the exception. Its small ions travel deepest, and over hours they work toward the center. Salt dissolves some muscle proteins, which helps the meat hold onto moisture and season more evenly. That's why salty liquids like soy sauce or a brine do most of a marinade's real work.

Acids such as vinegar, citrus, or wine only change the outer layer. Left too long, they can make the surface mushy or chalky. Enzymes from pineapple, papaya, or kiwi act the same way. They break down the surface aggressively, so overnight use can turn the outside to paste.

Oil doesn't soak in at all. Its job is to carry fat-soluble flavors from garlic, herbs, and spices onto the surface. Those aromatic molecules are too large to travel far anyway. Sugars stay on the outside too, where they help with browning.

In practice, a marinade seasons and flavors the surface rather than the whole cut. For deeper effects, rely on salt or score the meat.
